items.prompt: A client sends a request with a typo in the path and gets back a 404. Which range does that status code belong to?
choices: 1xx — informational
2xx — success
4xx — client error
5xx — server error
items.explanation: 4xx means the client's request itself was the problem (in this case, asking for a path that doesn't exist) — the server understood the request fine, it just has nothing to return for it.
items.reference:
2xx

request worked

3xx

go look elsewhere

4xx

client's mistake

5xx

server's mistake

Why: the first digit tells you who's at fault (or that nobody is) before you even read the rest.
items.learnMore:
Status code ranges

Grouped by first digit, not memorized one by one.

RangeWho acts nextExample
2xxNobody — it worked200 OK
3xxClient follows the new location301 Moved Permanently
4xxClient fixes the request404 Not Found
5xxServer owner fixes the server503 Service Unavailable

Common mistake

Treating a 3xx as an error. A redirect is a normal, successful instruction to look somewhere else — not a failure.

items.explanation: 5xx means the server side failed to do its job even though the request itself was valid — a dead dependency (like the database here) is exactly the server's problem, not the client's, so it's not 4xx.

items.prompt: A load balancer sends request #1 to server A and request #2 (from the same user, milliseconds later) to server B, with no coordination between A and B. Why does this work?
choices: Servers A and B share a database of active users
Each request carries everything needed to answer it — HTTP is stateless by default
The load balancer secretly forwards state between servers
It only works because both requests use the same TCP connection
items.explanation: Neither server needs to remember the other request exists — statelessness is exactly what makes this kind of load balancing possible without coordination.
items.reference:
State on the server

needs coordination between servers

State in the request

any server can answer it alone

Why: HTTP puts everything a server needs to answer inside the request itself, so no server has to remember a prior one.
items.learnMore:
Why statelessness matters operationally

A self-contained request is what makes horizontal scaling boring instead of hard.

ConsequenceBecause of statelessness
Load balancingAny server can take any request, no session affinity required
CachingSame request → same response, so a cache can safely replay it
TestingYou can curl one endpoint in isolation and get a meaningful answer

Common mistake

Assuming statelessness means apps can't have logins or carts. They can — the app layers state back on top (cookies, tokens); HTTP itself just doesn't require it.

items.prompt: Why can you `curl` a public GET endpoint and get a meaningful answer without "logging in" first?
choices: curl automatically authenticates as a guest user
The endpoint remembers curl from previous requests
The request itself contains everything the server needs to answer it — nothing prior is required
GET requests are exempt from needing a connection
items.explanation: Statelessness means a request is self-contained — the server doesn't need any memory of what came before to produce a response, so there's nothing to "log in" to unless the application itself layers auth on top.

items.prompt: Which three parts make up every HTTP request?
choices: URL, cookie, session ID
Request line, headers, optional body
Method, status code, reason phrase
Host, port, protocol
items.explanation: A request line (method + path + version), headers (metadata), and an optional body — the same three-part shape a response mirrors, just with a status line instead of a request line up top.
items.reference:
Request

request line, headers, body?

Response

status line, headers, body?

Why: a response mirrors a request's shape — only the first line's job changes (say what you want vs. say what happened).
items.learnMore:
Three parts, both directions

Every HTTP message — request or response — has the same three-part shape.

PartIn a requestIn a response
First lineMethod + path + versionVersion + status + reason
HeadersKey/value metadataKey/value metadata
BodyOptionalOptional

Common mistake

Thinking a body is mandatory. GET requests and many responses (like 204 No Content) legitimately have none.

items.prompt: A response's first line changes what it communicates compared to a request's first line. What does a response's first line (the status line) contain instead of a method and path?

The request line that triggered it, unchanged
A timestamp and a checksum
items.explanation: A status line says what happened (version + status code + reason phrase, e.g. "HTTP/1.1 200 OK") the same way a request line says what's wanted (method + path + version) — same shape, different job.

items.prompt: A route is defined as `GET /delete-account`. What's actually wrong with this, given that GET requests work fine over HTTP?
choices: Nothing — GET can trigger any server-side effect the code wants
It violates GET's convention of "no side effects expected," which browsers/proxies may rely on (e.g. prefetching or retrying GETs freely)
GET requests cannot reach server-side handlers at all
The path must start with /api for DELETE-like actions
items.explanation: Methods encode intent by convention, not by network enforcement. Browsers, proxies, and crawlers treat GET as safe to prefetch or retry — a GET route with real side effects can get triggered accidentally by exactly that assumption.
items.reference:
GET

fetch, no side effects expected

POST

create / submit, side effects expected

Why: the method states intent by convention — the network doesn't enforce it, the server's code has to actually honor it.
items.learnMore:
Methods are a convention, not a network rule

Nothing in TCP stops a GET handler from deleting data — the server's own code has to respect the convention.

MethodIntended for
GETFetch, no side effects
POSTCreate / submit
PUT / PATCHReplace / update
DELETERemove

Common mistake

Assuming a method's semantics are enforced by the protocol. A `GET /delete-everything` route is bad practice, not a network error — proxies and browsers that prefetch/retry GETs assuming safety will happily trigger it.

items.prompt: What's the difference in intent between POST and PUT?
choices: POST is for reading, PUT is for writing
POST is generally for creating/submitting; PUT is generally for replacing/updating an existing resource
They are exact synonyms with no convention difference
PUT can only be used for file uploads
items.explanation: By convention, POST usually creates or submits something new, while PUT/PATCH usually replace or update something that already exists — again, a convention the server's routing and handlers choose to honor, not something the transport layer enforces.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Why can a raw `nc example.com 80` session, with a hand-typed request, get a real response back from a web server?
choices: nc has a built-in HTTP client that browsers also secretly use
HTTP is just text sent over a TCP connection — nc can send that text manually, same as any HTTP client would
It only works for HTTPS, not plain HTTP
Servers give nc special permissions
items.explanation: There's no hidden binary layer — HTTP messages are plain text over a TCP connection, so anything that can open a TCP connection and write text to it (nc, a browser, curl) can speak HTTP.
items.reference:
📄 A request is text — readable in a terminal, no binary framing
🔌 Sent over TCP — same transport curl, browsers, and `nc` all use

Why: there's no hidden binary protocol underneath — what you see in `curl -v` is genuinely the whole message.
items.learnMore:
HTTP has no magic underneath it

A browser, curl, and a raw `nc` connection are all doing the same thing at the wire level.

ToolWhat it sends
BrowserPlain HTTP text, built for you
curlSame text, shown with -v
nc (netcat)Same text, typed by hand

Common mistake

Thinking HTTPS changes this. TLS encrypts the bytes on the wire, but the HTTP message itself is still the exact same readable text underneath the encryption.

items.prompt: `curl -v` prints out the exact request and response text it sent and received. What does that prove about HTTP?
choices: curl has debug hooks into a private binary protocol
The request/response really is human-readable text with no hidden framing underneath — curl is just showing you exactly what went over the wire
curl converts binary HTTP into text for display purposes only
This only works because curl is written in C
items.explanation: curl -v isn't decoding or reconstructing anything — it's printing the literal bytes sent and received, because HTTP already is text. That's what makes it debuggable with nothing but a terminal.

items.prompt: A hand-crafted raw HTTP request is missing the blank line between its headers and its body. What actually goes wrong?
choices: Nothing — servers ignore blank lines entirely
The parser can't tell where headers end and the body begins, since the blank line is the only separator
The request is automatically rejected with a 301
The body gets sent as an extra header instead
items.explanation: The blank line (\r\n\r\n) is the field separator between headers and body — without it, a parser has no signal that headers are finished, and will typically keep treating incoming bytes as more header lines.
items.reference:
GET /x HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
<blank line>
(body, if any)

Why: the blank line is the only signal that tells a parser "headers are done, body starts here."
items.learnMore:
The blank line is a field separator, not decoration

Without it, a parser has no way to know where headers end and the body begins.

SequenceMeaning
End of one header line
End of all headers — body starts right after

Common mistake

Hand-building raw requests/responses and forgetting the final blank line — a compliant parser will keep waiting for more header lines that never come.

The sequence \r\n\r\n (an empty line)
The TCP connection closing
A `Body:` label

Every header line ends in

, and whatever comes after it is the body.

items.prompt: Why does HTTP/1.1 keep-alive make writing a request parser harder than assuming one request per connection?
choices: Keep-alive requests use a different text format
The parser must re-synchronize on request boundaries itself, since the connection no longer closes to mark where one request ends
Keep-alive requests can't have a body
Keep-alive is only used for responses, never requests
items.explanation: Without a close to rely on, the parser has to track exactly how many bytes belonged to the current request (via Content-Length or chunked encoding) and treat anything after that as the start of the next one.
items.reference:
Connection: close

connection ends → boundary is free

keep-alive

parser must track boundaries itself

Why: without a close to rely on, the parser is the only thing that knows where one request ends and the next begins.
items.learnMore:
What keep-alive changes about parsing

One connection now carries an unbounded stream of requests, not just one.

ModeHow the parser knows a request ended
Connection: closeSocket closes — read until EOF
keep-aliveContent-Length / chunked encoding tells it exactly

Common mistake

Assuming one `data` event equals one full request. A pipelined connection can deliver two requests in a single chunk, or split one request across several chunks.

items.prompt: A keep-alive connection delivers two full requests in a single TCP `data` event because the client pipelined them close together. What must a correct parser do?
choices: Discard the second request — only one request per data event is supported
Consume exactly the first request's bytes, then loop and check the remaining buffer for another complete request, instead of assuming the chunk is one request
Close the connection and ask the client to resend
Merge both requests into one before handling them
items.explanation: A parser has to peel off exactly one request's worth of bytes at a time and keep checking what's left in the buffer — a single `data` event is not a reliable unit of "one request" under keep-alive/pipelining.

items.prompt: A proxy automatically retries a failed `DELETE /articles/42` request, assuming DELETE is idempotent. The server's handler, written poorly, deletes the *next* article in the table each time it's called instead of checking if 42 already exists. What does this expose about idempotency?
choices: Idempotency is guaranteed by the network layer, so this can't actually happen
Idempotency is only a convention the handler's code has to honor — nothing in HTTP forces DELETE to behave idempotently
DELETE requests are never safe to retry under any circumstances
This is a bug in the proxy, not the handler
items.explanation: The DELETE method is supposed to be idempotent by convention, which is exactly why proxies/retry logic feel safe resending it — but that safety only holds if the server's actual implementation honors the convention, which this one doesn't.
items.reference:
📜 The convention — GET/PUT/DELETE, called twice, should have the same effect as once
⚠️ Not enforced — a badly written handler can still make a GET destructive

Why: the convention exists so retry logic can safely resend idempotent methods — but it only holds if the handler actually honors it.
items.learnMore:
Idempotency is a promise, not a guarantee

It's a contract the handler's author has to uphold — nothing in HTTP or TCP enforces it.

MethodSupposed to be idempotent?
GETYes
PUTYes
DELETEYes
POSTNo — repeating it may create a duplicate

Common mistake

Assuming a retry library is always safe to auto-retry any request. It's only safe for methods the handler actually implemented idempotently — retrying a broken POST-as-side-effect handler can double the effect.

items.prompt: Why is it specifically safe, by convention, for a browser or HTTP client to automatically retry a failed GET request, but not a failed POST request?
choices: GET requests are smaller in size, so retries are cheaper
GET is supposed to have no side effects and be idempotent, so repeating it should be harmless — POST commonly creates something, so repeating it may duplicate that effect
POST requests are encrypted differently and can't be resent
There's no real difference — both are equally safe to retry
items.explanation: The idempotency convention is precisely what lets automatic retry logic treat GET as safe to resend without asking — POST carries no such promise, so blindly retrying a POST can create a duplicate order, comment, or charge.
items.reference:
📜 The convention — GET/PUT/DELETE, called twice, should have the same effect as once
⚠️ Not enforced — a badly written handler can still make a GET destructive

Why: the convention exists so retry logic can safely resend idempotent methods — but it only holds if the handler actually honors it.

items.prompt: TCP delivers a raw stream of bytes with no built-in concept of "message boundaries." Given that, what problem does the `Content-Length` header actually solve?
choices: It compresses the body to save bandwidth
It tells the receiver exactly how many bytes to read as the body, since TCP alone gives no way to know where the body ends
It verifies the body hasn't been corrupted in transit
It's purely informational and has no effect on parsing
items.explanation: TCP is just a byte stream — without an explicit length (or chunked encoding), the receiver has no way to know when the body is finished versus when more bytes are still coming.
items.reference:
🌊 TCP — a byte stream, no built-in message boundaries
📏 Content-Length — HTTP's explicit "read exactly this many bytes" instruction

Why: TCP alone can't tell a reader where a message ends — HTTP has to say so explicitly.
items.learnMore:
Two ways to mark where a body ends

Both exist because a receiver has no other way to know when to stop reading.

MechanismWhen it's used
Content-LengthThe full body size is known upfront
Transfer-Encoding: chunkedThe body is streamed and its total size isn't known yet

Common mistake

Computing Content-Length from a string's character count instead of its actual byte count — wrong for any body with multi-byte UTF-8 characters (see L3).

items.prompt: A server wants to stream a response body whose total size isn't known in advance (e.g. a live-generated report). Since it can't supply an accurate `Content-Length` upfront, what's the alternative that still lets the receiver know where the body ends?
choices: Omit any length information — the receiver just guesses
Transfer-Encoding: chunked, which marks the end of the body explicitly without needing the total size upfront
Always close the TCP connection immediately after the headers
Send the body twice so the receiver can compare
items.explanation: Chunked encoding sends the body in labeled, self-describing chunks and a final zero-length chunk to mark the end — it solves the same "where does this end" problem as Content-Length, but without requiring the full size to be known in advance.
items.reference:
🌊 TCP — a byte stream, no built-in message boundaries
📏 Content-Length — HTTP's explicit "read exactly this many bytes" instruction

Why: TCP alone can't tell a reader where a message ends — HTTP has to say so explicitly.
items.learnMore:

Both exist because a receiver has no other way to know when to stop reading.

MechanismWhen it's used

Common mistake

Computing Content-Length from a string's character count instead of its actual byte count — wrong for any body with multi-byte UTF-8 characters (see L3).

items.prompt: A monitoring check only verifies that a health endpoint returns `200 OK`. A bug causes the endpoint to always return 200 with an empty body, even when the underlying service has crashed. What does this expose about status codes?
choices: This is impossible — a 200 always means the request succeeded correctly
A status code is a claim the server makes, not a guaranteed fact about the body's correctness — checking only the code, never the body, can miss a real outage
Empty bodies are automatically converted to a 5xx by the server
The bug is in the monitoring tool's HTTP library, not the check's design
items.explanation: Nothing enforces that a 200's body is actually correct — the status line and the body are set independently by the server's code. A monitoring check that only reads the status code is trusting the server's word for it, and this scenario is exactly where that trust fails.
items.reference:
Status-only check

200 OK, empty body → looks fine, isn't

Status + body check

200 OK, but body shape is wrong → caught

Why: a status code is whatever the server chose to send — trusting it blindly means trusting the server's word for it.
items.learnMore:
A status code is a claim, not a fact

Nothing forces the status code and the body to actually agree with each other.

ScenarioStatus-only monitoringStatus + body validation
Crashed service, gateway still returns 200Misses itCatches it

Common mistake

Writing client code (or health checks) that only branches on `response.status`, without ever validating that the body actually matches what a healthy response should look like.

items.prompt: Why should client code that only checks `if (response.status === 200)` and never inspects the body be treated as a real risk, not just overly cautious advice?
choices: Because status 200 is deprecated in modern HTTP
Because a 200 with a malformed or wrong-shaped body is technically still a 200 — the status code doesn't guarantee the body is what the client expects
Because status codes are optional and can be missing entirely
Because 200 only applies to GET requests
items.explanation: A status code communicates the server's own claim about the outcome — it says nothing about whether the body it sent alongside that claim is actually well-formed or correct. Code that trusts the status alone is skipping the only check that would catch a mismatch.

items.prompt: Two teams both run the same crashed service behind a gateway that still answers 200 for every request. Team A's alert checks status code only; Team B's alert also validates the response body's shape. Which team detects the outage faster, and why?
choices: Team A, because status-only checks run faster
Team B, because validating the body catches the mismatch between "claims to be fine" and "is actually fine" that a status-only check can't see
Neither — status codes always reflect the true state of the service
They detect it at the same time, since both check the same endpoint
items.explanation: Team B's check looks past the server's claim (the status code) to the actual evidence (the body). Team A's check trusts the claim alone, so a service that keeps claiming success while actually failing slips right past it.

items.prompt: A team adds an in-memory cache on each server instance that stores "the last thing this user did," and now users get inconsistent behavior depending on which server handles their next request. What architectural property did this break?
choices: TLS termination
Statelessness — request handling started depending on server-local memory instead of being fully determined by the request itself
The Content-Length header
HTTP method semantics
items.explanation: As soon as a server needs its own memory of a prior request to answer correctly, requests are no longer interchangeable across servers — which is exactly the property a load balancer relies on to route freely.
items.reference:
⚖️ Load balancing — any server can take any request
🗄️ Caching — same request always deserves the same cached response

Why: both only work because the request alone determines the response, with nothing left implicit on the server side.
items.learnMore:
Statelessness is an architecture decision, not just a trivia fact

It's the property that lets infrastructure treat servers as interchangeable.

CapabilityRequires
Round-robin load balancingNo server-side memory of prior requests
Response cachingRequest alone determines the response

Common mistake

Adding in-memory server-side session state "just for this one feature," which quietly breaks load balancer interchangeability until sticky sessions are bolted back on.

items.prompt: Why can a CDN cache the response to `GET /articles/42` and correctly serve that same cached response to a different user later, without asking the origin server again?
choices: CDNs re-run the request against the origin server every time regardless
Because the request alone (in principle) determines the response — same request in, same response out, so a cached copy stays valid without needing per-user coordination
GET requests are exempt from caching rules by convention
The CDN silently authenticates as the origin server
items.explanation: Caching relies on the same statelessness property as load balancing: if the response is fully determined by the request, a cached response is valid for anyone who sends that same request — no per-user memory required.
items.reference:
⚖️ Load balancing — any server can take any request
🗄️ Caching — same request always deserves the same cached response

Why: both only work because the request alone determines the response, with nothing left implicit on the server side.

items.prompt: A request line is `GET /articles/42 HTTP/1.1` and a status line is `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`. Both have three space-separated fields — what's the actual parallel between them?
choices: There is no real parallel, it's a coincidence
Method↔version, path↔status code, version↔reason phrase describe the same structural position, just serving opposite purposes (what's wanted vs. what happened)
Both lines always have identical content
The status line is just the request line echoed back
items.explanation: Both are three-field first lines of their message. A request line states what's wanted (method + path + version); a status line states what happened (version + status + reason) — same shape, mirrored job.

tests.description: parses a basic GET request line
parses a root path

items.explanation: The three fields of a request line are separated by single spaces in a fixed order, so a plain .split(" ") destructures cleanly into method/path/version — no regex needed for the well-formed case. items.reference:
GET /articles/42 HTTP/1.1

Why: a request line is three space-separated fields in a fixed order — method, path, version.

Trying to split the query string out of the path at this stage. The request-line parser's job is just the three fields — splitting `?query=params` out of the path is a separate, later step, not part of request-line parsing.

items.prompt: Write parseHeaders(lines) that takes an array of raw header lines and returns an object with lowercased header names and trimmed values.

tests.description: lowercases header names
parses multiple headers
empty input gives an empty object

items.explanation: Header names are case-insensitive per the HTTP spec, so lowercasing on the way in means later code can always look up headers["content-type"] regardless of how the client capitalized it. Using indexOf(":") rather than split(":") specifically preserves any additional colons inside the value itself (like a port number in a URL).
items.reference:
✅ "Host: example.com" → key "host", value "example.com"
⚠️ a line with no colon → malformed, skip it rather than crash

Why: header names are case-insensitive by spec, so lowercasing on parse avoids missed lookups later.

Turning header lines into a lookup object

Three small rules, each defending against a real malformed-input case.

RuleDefends against
Lowercase the name"Host" vs "host" lookup mismatches
Trim the valueStray whitespace after the colon

Common mistake

Splitting a header line on ":" without limiting to the first colon — a value like "Location: http://x.com:8080/" has more than one colon, and a naive split would corrupt it.

trims extra whitespace around the value

items.prompt: Write buildResponse(status, reason, bodyObj) that returns a full raw HTTP response string: a status line, Content-Type: application/json, a correct Content-Length (real UTF-8 byte count of the JSON body), a blank line, then the JSON body. Use \r\n line endings.

tests.description: status line is correct
Content-Length matches the real byte count of the JSON body
the body is appended after the blank line

items.explanation: The Content-Length has to be derived from the actual bytes being sent — JSON.stringify(bodyObj) first, then a real UTF-8 byte count via TextEncoder, not the object itself or the string's .length. Getting this wrong means the header promises a length that doesn't match what follows it, which is exactly the kind of mismatch that truncates or hangs a receiver reading exactly that many bytes.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 11
<blank line>
{"ok":true}

Why: Content-Length must equal the real byte count of exactly what follows it — get it wrong and the client truncates or hangs.
items.learnMore:
Building a response by hand

Every promise the headers make has to match the bytes actually written after them.

PartMust match
Status lineThe status + reason actually passed in
Content-LengthReal UTF-8 byte count of the body written after it

Computing Content-Length from the object before JSON.stringify, or from .length instead of a real byte count — either way the promised length stops matching what's actually written.

items.prompt: Write findHeaderEnd(buffer) that returns the index of the \r\n\r\n sequence marking the end of the headers, or -1 if it hasn't arrived yet.

tests.description: finds the boundary in a complete head
returns -1 when the blank line hasn't arrived yet

items.explanation: indexOf returns the position of the first match, or -1 if the sequence isn't present at all — which maps exactly onto the two states a streaming parser needs to distinguish: "headers are complete, I can parse them now" versus "still waiting for more bytes." A parser that skips this check and assumes the buffer is always a complete request will intermittently truncate requests split across TCP packets.
items.reference:
✅ full headers arrived → index of \r\n\r\n found
⏳ only partial headers so far → -1, wait for more data

Why: TCP can deliver a request split across multiple chunks — the parser has to keep checking, not assume one chunk is the whole thing.
items.learnMore:
Finding the header/body boundary in a growing buffer

The same three outcomes matter every time new bytes arrive.

Buffer stateResult
Headers not fully arrived yet-1
Headers complete, maybe more afterIndex of the first \r\n\r\n

Common mistake

Assuming the first `data` event is always the complete request. A slow client or a large header block can split arrival across several events — the parser has to re-check the buffer, not trust the first chunk alone.

items.prompt: Write sanitizeHeaderValue(value) that strips any \r or \n characters from a header value before it's written into a raw response, preventing CRLF injection / header splitting.

tests.description: a clean value is returned unchanged
an injected CRLF plus a forged header line is stripped out

items.explanation: A raw header block is built by string concatenation, so any \r or \n an attacker manages to smuggle into a value is indistinguishable from a real line break to whatever writes the response — stripping both characters removes the ability to forge a new header line or split the response entirely, regardless of what text surrounds them.

🚨 unsanitized: userInput containing → injects extra headers
✅ sanitized: and stripped before ever reaching a header line

Why: a raw header block is just concatenated text — an attacker-controlled inside a value can forge extra header lines.

CRLF injection / response splitting

Never concatenate untrusted input directly into a raw header block.

InputRisk if unsanitized
A redirect URL from a query paramAttacker injects a fake Set-Cookie or a whole second response

Only checking for as a literal two-character substring instead of removing and independently — some clients or proxies normalize lone or into a full line break too.
